paragraphs: Children in care in Aldershot are the responsibility of Hampshire County Council, whose own fostering service works alongside the independent agencies shown above. The council describes its service as a community of more than 450 fostering households supported by around 60 staff, and says it is rated outstanding by Ofsted. Since July 2024 it has also been part of Local Authority Fostering South East, a partnership of 20 councils funded by the Department for Education; when it launched, Hampshire said another child came into its care every 12 hours.

Local support matters for carers here. Hampshire's carers belong to the Hampshire Hive, a network of local groups offering support meetings, one-to-one help and family events, and the council's Hive page lists three separate groups for Aldershot and Farnborough. Carers also have an out-of-hours helpline, a buddy carer and free FosterTalk membership for legal, counselling and money advice.

The council has a page for armed forces families. It sets no minimum time living in Hampshire before you apply, but asks approved carers to expect to stay in the county for at least two years, because approval does not move with you and a child cannot follow a carer on a posting. People in Single Living Accommodation cannot foster, though they can apply to move to Service Families Accommodation, and visits on base can be arranged with an escorted pass.

To apply you need to be over 21, with no upper age limit, and a spare bedroom is essential. You can rent, you do not need to drive, and a criminal record is not an automatic bar. Assessment usually takes four to six months. Allowances are paid for each child by age, with skills fees on top as you train. In Aldershot, it is worth speaking to the council and two or three of the agencies above before you decide.
